summary: Selene's Compass (named after the Greek goddess of the moon) is a web application helps mission planners, educators and anyone interested find statistics about lunar lands sites by making the experience as visual and interactive as possible. It shows what a lander site would actually experience when the Sun is up to give it power, and when Earth is in view for a direct radio link home. The application is split into four components. The first is a Google Maps style model where users can select from existing landing sites or choose their own. The second is a first person perspective from the chosen site so that users can see the earth/sun cycles as if they were at the site itself as well as other data. The third is a site comparison tool to allow users to compare various traits from each site against one another to be able to find optimal conditions. Finally, there is an explanation page which goes through the math, references and data that was used for the application to help understand exactly how the models and approximations are found allowing for further exploration into the field if the user is so inclined.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Selene's Compass is a web application that helps people find and compare lunar landing sites by showing where the Sun and Earth are from any spot on the Moon, at any date and time. This matters because a lander needs the Sun for power and Earth in view to talk to home. At the Moon's south pole both of these sit really close to the horizon, so a ridge kilometres away can be the difference between having power and contact or not having them at all.

The application is split into four parts. The first is Choose site, where you can spin a 3D Moon or use a top-down map of the south pole. You can pick from 16 existing sites, like Apollo 11 and 17, Chang'e 4 and 6, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, IM-1, IM-2, Blue Ghost and VIPER's planned site, along with some of the best-lit points from published south pole studies. You can also drop your own pin or type in coordinates, and save your own sites with your own names. There is also a plot that stacks 13 lunar days on top of each other, so you can see how the light changes over a whole year.

The second is Analyse, which puts you on the surface at the site, looking at the real skyline with the Sun and Earth where they would actually be. Earth even shows its real face and phase. You can press Play to watch them move along the horizon. It also shows how long until sunset or Earthset, a timeline of when each one is in view over the next 29.5 days, and a calculator for solar power and how big a battery you would need to get through the longest dark stretch.

The third is Compare, which lets you put up to 24 sites and dates side by side and filter and sort them. The last is About, which goes through all of the maths the app uses, every source and what was taken from it, how the results were checked, and a full list of what the tool can't do.


What benefits does it have?

Tools like JPL Horizons, Quickmap and Moon Trek already have this kind of data, but they're built for detailed analysis and can be hard to use if you just want to quickly compare a few sites and dates. Selene's Compass puts all of that on one screen. You can see straight away which sites have the most sunlight, the most time in sight of Earth, and the longest stretches without either. Missions get delayed all the time, so being able to pick the same site at a later date and instantly see what the delay costs you is a big one.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The hope is that it helps mission planners take a quick first look at their options to plan or when plans change, before they move on to the more detailed tools. It's also meant to help students and the public understand why landing at the south pole is so hard. Watching the Sun skim along a ridge and disappear for days explains it a lot better than a table of numbers does. And because the About page goes through all of the maths and sources, people can dig further into the field if they're interested.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Coding: TypeScript, HTML and CSS
  • Libraries: Three.js for the 3D views and Astronomy Engine for the positions of the Sun, Earth and Moon
  • Build and testing: Vite to build it, and Vitest and Puppeteer for testing
  • Data preparation: Node.js and sharp to prepare the NASA data
  • Hosting: Cloudflare
  • NASA data: the LRO LOLA south pole elevation data, the CGI Moon Kit from NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio, the Blue Marble images of Earth, and JPL Horizons for checking
  • Hardware: personal computer
  • AI: Claude Code by Anthropic (disclosed in the app and the README on GitHub)

How is your project creative?

The main contribution is how the application has taken existing complicated data (at least for a non-scientific audience) and tries to illustrate it simply by using visual aids such as 3D models, 1st person perspective views and graphs. There was also a big attempt at making the choice of landing site's data as easy to get to as possible to remove friction for the user. Finally, for the non-technical audience (or even for the technical audience) there was a serious attempt at making all math and approximations as transparent and easy to understand as possible to allow people to understand exactly how something like optimal lunar landing site parameters are calculated. The hope is that this page also encourages people to follow the reference links to further engage with the field.

What factors did your team consider?

The big thing I had to balance was making it technical enough for people in this field to actually use, but simple enough that people who aren't in the field can still understand what's going on. Early on it was information overload, so I changed it so that the main answer shows first and the detail is tucked away until you open it. Nothing is removed, it's just not all thrown at you at once.

I also wanted to be really transparent about what the app can and can't do. It's a planning and teaching tool, not a flight tool, and the About page says that clearly, along with things like where there isn't real terrain and where the maths is only an approximation. For the sources, I only cited what I could actually look at, and anything I couldn't read directly is marked that way.

Privacy was another one. I wanted each person to have their own space, so nothing is stored on a server and one person's saved sites never show up for anyone else. Finally, I made sure it works on phones, can be used with a keyboard, and respects reduced-motion settings.
